questions.question_text: A school wants to find out students' favourite sports. It surveys only members of the school football team. Why may the results be unrepresentative?

options.text: Football team members may have different sporting preferences from other students
Every student at the school has been included
options.why: Only football team members were surveyed; students outside the team were excluded.

options.text: The sample is representative because everyone surveyed attends the school
options.why: Belonging to the population does not make this selected group representative of all students.

options.text: The results prove that all students prefer football
options.why: Preferences in the football team cannot establish the preferences of students who were not surveyed.

questions.solution_text:
Football team members may be more interested in football than other students. Surveying only this group leaves out other students' preferences.
Football team members may have different sporting preferences from other students.

questions.question_text: A class uses a new spelling programme. Its mean test mark increases from $13$ to $17$. What other information would help show whether the programme caused the improvement?

options.text: How marks changed for a comparable control group without the programme, using comparable tests over the same period
Only the highest mark after the programme
options.why: One highest mark does not show whether students would improve without the programme.

options.text: Whether the students liked the programme's name
options.why: Liking the name does not provide a comparison of improvement with and without the programme.

options.text: The same class's final mean mark reported a second time
options.why: Repeating the final mean adds no control group and cannot separate the programme's effect from improvement that might occur anyway.

questions.solution_text:
Marks may improve over time without the programme. Compare the change with a comparable group that did not use it, keeping other relevant conditions the same.
How marks changed for a comparable control group without the programme, using comparable tests over the same period.

questions.question_text: A survey asks: 'How often do you read?' The choices are 'A little' and 'A lot'. Which criticism is valid?

options.text: There is no time frame, and the choices may mean different amounts to different people
The question clearly asks for the number of hours read during the past week
options.why: Neither hours nor the past week is specified in the question.

options.text: The choices give exact numerical amounts
options.why: 'A little' and 'A lot' are vague descriptions rather than exact amounts.

options.text: The question tells respondents that reading is excellent
options.why: The question contains no praise or preferred answer; its stated faults are ambiguity and vague choices.

questions.solution_text:
Respondents may think about different periods when answering. They may also interpret 'A little' and 'A lot' differently.
There is no time frame, and the choices may mean different amounts to different people.

questions.question_text: A survey asks: 'Don't you agree that our wonderful new playground is excellent?' Which replacement question and response section is most suitable?

options.text: 'How would you rate the new playground?' Choices: Very good, Good, Neither good nor poor, Poor, Very poor, Have not used it
'How excellent is our wonderful playground?' Choices: Excellent, Very excellent
options.why: The wording still praises the playground, and both choices require a positive opinion.

options.text: 'How would you rate the new playground?' Choices: Excellent, Good
options.why: The wording is neutral, but the choices provide no way to express a neutral or negative opinion.

options.text: 'Do you agree that the playground is terrible?' Choices: Yes, No
options.why: Calling the playground terrible introduces emotional language that encourages a negative opinion.

questions.solution_text:
Remove the praise from the question and provide choices for positive, neutral and negative opinions, as well as people who have not used the playground.
'How would you rate the new playground?' with the full range of response choices is most suitable.

questions.question_text: A study of business success includes only shops still operating after six years. Why may its conclusion be misleading?

options.text: It excludes shops that closed, so looking only at survivors may overstate success
Shops that closed are included automatically
options.why: The study explicitly includes only shops still operating.

options.text: Operating for six years proves that every new shop succeeds
options.why: The survival of the included shops says nothing about excluded shops that failed.

options.text: The sample must represent all new shops because it includes successful shops
options.why: Representing success requires considering failures as well as survivors.

questions.solution_text:
Shops that failed during the six years are missing. Considering only the shops that survived can make business success appear more common than it is.
This is survivorship bias.

questions.question_text: A survey asks how many hours students spent online yesterday. Its only choices are '$0$–$3$ hours', '$3$–$6$ hours' and '$6$–$9$ hours'. Which criticism is correct?

options.text: The boundaries overlap at $3$ and $6$ hours, and there is no choice for more than $9$ hours
There is no time frame
options.why: The question specifies yesterday, which is a clear time frame.

options.text: Exactly $3$ hours fits only the first choice
options.why: Both the first and second intervals include the boundary value $3$.

options.text: The final choice includes all amounts above $9$ hours
options.why: The final choice ends at $9$ hours and does not include larger amounts.

questions.solution_text:
Exactly $3$ hours fits the first two intervals, and exactly $6$ hours fits the last two. A student who spent more than $9$ hours online has no suitable choice.
The boundaries overlap at $3$ and $6$ hours, and there is no choice for more than $9$ hours.

questions.question_text:
A government agency mails $2000$ detailed forms asking citizens about their private financial debts.
Only $50$ completed forms are returned ($2.5\%$ response rate), and the agency publishes the findings without contacting non-respondents.
What data collection fault has occurred?

options.text: A risk of non-response bias because very few selected citizens replied and no follow-up was attempted
Observer effect caused by visible camera surveillance
options.why: Mail surveys involve no camera surveillance or visible observer effect.

options.text: Instrument measurement error from faulty electronic timing gates
options.why: Electronic timing gates relate to physical sports measurements, not mail surveys.

options.text: Failure to provide a placebo control group
options.why: Surveys do not use medical placebo control groups.

questions.solution_text:
$50\div2000\times100\%=2.5\%$ replied, so $97.5\%$ did not.
The respondents' debt levels may differ from those of non-respondents. Few replies and no follow-up leave this risk unchecked; the low rate alone does not prove which way the result is biased.
A risk of non-response bias because very few selected citizens replied and no follow-up was attempted.

questions.question_text: A cinema surveys only customers entering its own building. It asks: 'Do you agree that our cinema is much better than the other cinema?' The choices are 'Strongly agree', 'Agree' and 'Not sure'. Which statement correctly identifies faults in the question, response section and sample?

options.text: The question encourages agreement, there is no disagreement choice, and customers of this cinema may not represent all cinema-goers
The question is neutral, but the choices and sample are unsuitable
options.why: Describing the cinema as much better and asking for agreement encourages a favourable answer.

options.text: The question is leading, but 'Not sure' lets customers express disagreement
options.why: 'Not sure' expresses uncertainty; it does not let someone state that they disagree.

options.text: The question and choices are biased, but customers entering this cinema represent all cinema-goers
options.why: Customers entering this cinema may already prefer it and exclude people who choose other cinemas.

questions.solution_text:
The wording presents the cinema as better and encourages agreement. The choices omit disagreement. Surveying only its own customers may miss different views held by customers of other cinemas.
The question encourages agreement, there is no disagreement choice, and customers of this cinema may not represent all cinema-goers.
